::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p >.6", Sentence = "Responses did not vary with the number of habituation trials (p >.6)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: Theory of Mind (ToM) is central to human social cognition and is critical for successfully navigating the social world.
However, most work to date has explored explicit ToM in AI, particularly with large language models (LLMs), and has found mixed results.
In contrast, decades of developmental psychology research with human infants has found remarkable, early-emerging implicit ToM.
However, little work has explored implicit ToM in LLMs.
The current study investigates implicit social reasoning abilities in GPT-4 using model-facing versions of classic infant experiments.
In Experiment 1, we explored GPT-4's implicit ToM abilities across four social reasoning tasks adapted from infant paradigms.
In Experiment 2, we explored whether GPT-4 was capable of physical reasoning to contrast with social reasoning in Experiments 1 and 2.

Across these three experiments, our results suggest that there may be domain differences in GPT-4's reasoning abilities, such that GPT-4 struggled with social reasoning tasks despite performing very well on physical reasoning tasks.
These findings highlight the importance of systematic exploration of social reasoning in LLMs and provide insight into potential deficits in GPT-4's social reasoning abilities.
Theory of Mind (ToM) is the ability to reason about others' mental states, which allows us to understand others' beliefs, desires, and intentions.
ToM is a hallmark feature of human social cognition and is critical for successful human social interactions.

Decades of research from developmental psychology has explored ToM abilities across human development, finding that even very young infants have basic, early-emerging social reasoning abilities (see Wellman, 2018 for a review).
text.formatted: Decades of research from developmental psychology has explored ToM abilities across human development, finding that even very young infants have basic, early-emerging social reasoning abilities (see <ref type="bibr">Wellman, 2018</ref> for a review).

text.text: Given the interactional nature of AI systems with humans, which requires understanding human agents' intentions and beliefs, there has been a recent surge in interest in exploring whether LLMs also have ToM capabilities.

However, although much work has established that AI and, especially large language models (LLMs), are capable of other types of reasoning (e.g., Han et al., 2023; Bubeck et al., 2023; Stevenson et al., 2023), less work has explored whether AI systems are capable of reasoning about human intentions and beliefs.
text.formatted: However, although much work has established that AI and, especially large language models (LLMs), are capable of other types of reasoning (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Han et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bubeck et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Stevenson et al., 2023)</ref>, less work has explored whether AI systems are capable of reasoning about human intentions and beliefs.

text.text: Some work has explored this topic with LLMs by exclusively using explicit ToM, using tasks that require effortful reasoning about others' mental states.

However, these studies have found mixed results with LLMs on tasks that humans robustly succeed on (Baron-Cohen et al., 1985; Gandhi et al., 2023; Gu et al., 2024; Kosinski, 2024; Qiu et al., 2024; Strachan et al., 2024; Wellman et al., 2001; Ullman, 2023).
text.formatted: However, these studies have found mixed results with LLMs on tasks that humans robustly succeed on <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baron-Cohen et al., 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Gandhi et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Gu et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Kosinski, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Qiu et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Strachan et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Wellman et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Ullman, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Despite the focus on explicit ToM abilities in LLMs in the exploration of social reasoning capabilities in AI, research from developmental psychology reflects a different trend.
More specifically, a rich body of work with human infants has explored implicit ToM, or the fast, automatic, and effortless processing of others' mental states, rather than explicit ToM.

Many studies have provided evidence that even young infants have sophisticated, early-emerging implicit ToM abilities, such that they understand efficiency, effort, as well as the preferences and goals of others (Woodward, 1998; Gergely et al., 1995; Liu et al. 2017; Wellman et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Many studies have provided evidence that even young infants have sophisticated, early-emerging implicit ToM abilities, such that they understand efficiency, effort, as well as the preferences and goals of others <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Woodward, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Gergely et al., 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Liu et al. 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Wellman et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, infants' understanding of others can be characterized by two critical features.
First, infants only attribute mental states to agents, but do not do so to inanimate objects.

For example, infants only expect agents (e.g., a human hand) to engage in goal-directed actions, such as reaching for a specific toy, but do not attribute goal-directed actions to perceptually similar inanimate objects (e.g., a sponge carved to look like a hand; Woodward, 1998).
text.formatted: For example, infants only expect agents (e.g., a human hand) to engage in goal-directed actions, such as reaching for a specific toy, but do not attribute goal-directed actions to perceptually similar inanimate objects (e.g., a sponge carved to look like a hand; <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Woodward, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: Second, in addition to and distinct from their understanding of agents (e.g., people), infants also have a sophisticated understanding of the physical world.

For instance, previous work has found that infants by 4 or 5 months of age have a set of principles that guides their understanding of the physical world, such as object continuity, (that objects continue to exist in space and time; Spelke et al., 1995), solidity (i.e., that objects cannot pass through walls; Baillargeon, 1985), and support (i.e., that objects should fall if not properly supported from beneath; Baillargeon et al., 1992).

text.text: How do these findings from human development relate to AI and LLMs?

Theories of cognitive development have proposed that early-emerging implicit ToM abilities in infants and young children provide the foundation for later-developing explicit ToM abilities (Aschersleben et al., 2008; Wellman et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Theories of cognitive development have proposed that early-emerging implicit ToM abilities in infants and young children provide the foundation for later-developing explicit ToM abilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Aschersleben et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Wellman et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Given this relationship between implicit and explicit ToM and the current state of social reasoning abilities in AI, this raises the question of whether LLMs' current lack of success on complex explicit ToM tasks may be related to a lack of more foundational implicit ToM abilities.
However, it remains unclear whether LLMs are capable of implicit social reasoning (though see Kosoy et al., 2023; Ruis et al., 2023; Stojnić et al., 2023).
text.formatted: However, it remains unclear whether LLMs are capable of implicit social reasoning (though see <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Kosoy et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Ruis et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Stojnić et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The current study aims to explore this research gap by drawing upon the several decades of research with human infants documenting the core knowledge systems, specifically relating to physical and social reasoning, that guide infants' early understanding by using model-facing version of these well-replicated studies with LLMs.

In Experiment 1, we assessed GPT-4's (OpenAI, 2023) performance on model-facing replications of four human ToM infant studies, specifically covering: (1) goal-directed actions, (2) efficiency and rationality, (3) inferring preferences from intentional sampling, and (4) inferring the value of goals based on effort.

Given previous work finding improved performance from in-context learning, we also incorporated in-context learning in our assessments through habituation trials (which are trials repeatedly presented to human infants to familiarize them to the current context) to explore whether this supports model behavior (e.g., providing only one habituation trial which limits in-context learning vs. 14 habituation trials which allows for more).

In Experiment 2, we prompted GPT-4 with model-facing versions of classic infant physical reasoning studies (continuity, solidity, object permanence, and support) to contrast with social reasoning task performance.
2 Experiment 1: Social reasoning

All prompts followed the general structure as follows: (1a) Habituation Introduction briefly describing the setup of the task as adapted from the original infant experiments, (1b) Habituation Trials describing an event adapted from the original infant experiments, (2a) Test Introduction introducing any new changes to the scene that differed from the habituation phase, and (2b) Test Question prompting GPT-4 to make a binary choice judgement about the scenario based on two provided response options.
The order of response options was counterbalanced for all tasks (i.e., whether the correct response was option A or B).

Four classic infant social reasoning experiments were converted into text prompts for GPT-4, with each prompt assessing different fundamental early-emerging social principles in infants that involve distinct comparisons.
See Figure 2 for details and the Appendix for exact prompt examples.

Across the four physical reasoning tasks, our results suggest that GPT-4 reasons about physical principles similarly to infants.
Additionally, performance was very good from the outset of all tasks with little impact of in-context learning (i.e., no effect of number of habituation trials).
In our study, we designed a battery of model-facing implicit ToM and physical reasoning tasks adapted from well-established infant studies.

This approach allowed for a systematic exploration of implicit ToM, which are thought to be foundational for later emerging explicit ToM, in GPT-4 and provided a benchmark for comparing GPT-4 and infants.

Infant-like performance on these tasks can be determined based on two fundamental capabilities: (1) the ability to differentiate between agents and inanimate objects in social reasoning tasks and (2) a complex understanding of both agents and inanimate objects that are distinct from one another.
Overall, our results with GPT-4 suggest several deviations from human-like performance.
In Experiment 1, we assessed GPT-4's performance on different aspects of implicit ToM, all of which require different and distinct comparisons for human-like social reasoning.

Notably, GPT-4 failed to make these critical comparisons across all four tasks (i.e., agents vs. non-agents, rational vs. nonrational agents, intentional sampling of minority vs. majority objects, lower vs. higher effort when attributing values to goals), unlike infants who are able to successfully reason about all of these scenarios (Gergely et al., 1995; Liu et al., 2017; Wellman et al., 2016; Woodward et al., 1998).
text.formatted: Notably, GPT-4 failed to make these critical comparisons across all four tasks (i.e., agents vs. non-agents, rational vs. nonrational agents, intentional sampling of minority vs. majority objects, lower vs. higher effort when attributing values to goals), unlike infants who are able to successfully reason about all of these scenarios <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Gergely et al., 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Liu et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Wellman et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Woodward et al., 1998)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, in Experiment 1, where we assessed GPT-4's understanding of physical reasoning principles, GPT-4 performed comparably to infants on all four tasks.
One possible explanation for the stark domain differences in GPT-4's reasoning abilities is that GPT-4 failed to infer hidden belief states.
Implicit ToM tasks require multiple inferences involving hidden variables, which is not required for physical reasoning tasks.

For example, the Inferring Value from Goals task requires several layers of inference, such as understanding that one goal requires more effort to attain, more effort reflects a higher value, and agents prefer higher-value goals.
In contrast, the Continuity task only requires reasoning that an object placed behind the left screen should remain on the left when the screens are lifted.

These hidden belief states required for the implicit ToM tasks are not explicitly provided in our paradigms (and also not provided in infants studies), which may explain GPT-4's poor performance on these social reasoning tasks despite excellent performance on physical reasoning tasks.

This is also consistent with previous work suggesting LLMs failed to infer underlying belief states from corresponding behavior and fail to incorporate belief states when predicting future behavior (Qiu et al., 2024; Strachan et al., 2024).

text.text: However, there are several limitations and open questions that stem from this work.
Specifically, we only tested one LLM.
In order to more comprehensively understand potential domain differences in reasoning LLMs, more models should be tested on implicit ToM and physical reasoning tasks.
Additionally, we raise two important questions: (1) Infant studies are typically simplified; however, real life social reasoning depends on richer context.
It is possible that LLMs may perform better with additional, more naturalistic context than the infant paradigms provide.

(2) It is possible that GPT-4 may perform worse on more complex physical reasoning tasks that may be more comparable to the social reasoning tasks tested, such as an object permanence task that involves compression (e.g., Baillargeon, 1997).
text.formatted: (2) It is possible that GPT-4 may perform worse on more complex physical reasoning tasks that may be more comparable to the social reasoning tasks tested, such as an object permanence task that involves compression (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Baillargeon, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: In this type of task, the model would have to recognize that some objects are compressible (e.g., a sponge) whereas others are not (e.g., a wooden box), and use this information accordingly to determine that a rotating screen could rotate backwards farther when a compressible object is behind the screen compared to a non-compressible object.

Interestingly, preliminary results exploring more complex physical reasoning tasks suggest that GPT-4 continues to succeed on these more difficult physical reasoning tasks, further suggesting that the domain differences may not be due differences in task complexity.

Our findings highlight the importance of systematic exploration of reasoning abilities in LLMs across a broad range of tasks, including implicit ToM tasks which are foundational for human social reasoning.

Given the extensive research finding that humans have very early-emerging domainspecific systems of knowledge that differentiate between reasoning about agents versus objects, this raises the question of whether similar domain-specificity has emerged in LLMs' conceptual organization from the vast amount of training data these models receive.

Our study provides the foundation for future work to continue exploring domain-specificity and social reasoning in LLMs and other models (e.g., VLMs), to inform both the topics of improving AI and human conceptual development.
